fullText:
Surgeons aided by real-time analysis of camera footage that identified critical anatomy in brain to be avoided

Neurosurgeons in London have performed the world’s first successful AI-assisted operation to remove a brain tumour, saving the sight of a 48-year-old man, health officials have said.

The surgery was performed in May at the National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery (NHNN), part of University College London hospitals NHS foundation trust, but details were kept secret until Thursday while the patient, Rhys Hibbert, recovered.

While the surgical team remained in full control, the AI system analysed live camera footage during the operation, helping identify key structures such as nerves and blood vessels that should be avoided near the 11mm (0.4in) tumour on Hibbert’s pituitary gland.

“When I came round … I could see everything in the room clearly,” said Hibbert, who was able to walk independently without glasses or sticks within a week of the surgery.

He has since returned to work as a customer service manager. “It feels like I’ve got a 360‑degree panoramic view of everything around me,” he said.

The surgeons operated on Hibbert using new AI technology which helps to identify tiny anatomy in the brain by colour-coding important structures to help surgeons recognise them safely.

The hospital had previously used the technology as a research tool but the operation was the first time it had been used on a patient.

The pituitary gland, blood vessels and nerves controlling vision are tightly packed together, and “going a millimetre wrong can make a critical difference”, health officials said, potentially leading to blindness, stroke or death.

Dr Sophia Bano, an associate professor in robotics and AI at UCL and the technical lead for the AI system, said: “By learning from hundreds of surgical videos, [the system] has been exposed to a breadth of surgical examples that would take a surgeon many years to encounter.

“It is designed to help recognise critical anatomy, surgical instruments and tissue interactions in real time, supporting the surgeon during highly delicate procedures.”

Initially managed without surgery, Hibbert’s symptoms had worsened since his diagnosis in 2024, and included severe hormone imbalance and vision problems. Without the operation, he faced going blind, health officials said.

Hibbert, from Bedfordshire, said: “The NHNN was founded in 1859 … and was the world’s first dedicated neurosurgical hospital. So to me, it seems very fitting that the same hospital should also be the world’s first to carry out an AI-assisted neurosurgery.”

Prof Mike Lewis, the scientific director for innovation at the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR), which funded the operation as part of a clinical trial, said the “pioneering surgery” highlighted the potential of advanced AI to support surgeons and improve patient care.

title: London rollout of robotaxis delayed amid lack of guidance for firms to follow
description: Uber and Wayve had said they would start trips ‘later this summer’ but launch now looks unlikely this...
fullText:
Uber and Wayve had said they would start trips ‘later this summer’ but launch now looks unlikely this year

The rollout of robotaxis on the streets of London is unlikely to happen this year, as regulatory and technical hurdles push back the ambitious schedule set out by the UK government.

Only weeks ago Uber and London-based Wayve were granted the first minicab licences in the capital to allow them to offer self-driving taxi rides to paying customers – but with a human safety driver in place, for now – and said they would start trips “later this summer” before a full public launch.

In 2025, Heidi Alexander, the transport secretary, accelerated the proposed timeline for commercial trials of fully driverless taxi services by a year, announcing that they would start in the spring of this year.

However, progress has slowed in recent months and Transport for London (TfL) has still not published the guidance that companies wanting to offer services must follow to win its approval.

Last month, Christina Calderato, TfL’s director of strategy, told the London assembly’s transport committee that the transit authority would not be in a position to start accepting applications “for some time”.

She said: “I do not think we are in a rush to get [the guidelines] out. There is a huge amount of work going on behind the scenes.”

Uber and Wayve have said that more than 100,000 Londoners were on their waiting list for self-driving taxis.

They are racing against Google-owned Waymo and its Chinese equivalent, Baidu’s Apollo Go, to launch self-driving taxi services in London. Robotaxis are now available to hire in more than 20 cities across the US, China and the Middle East.

Earlier this month Zagreb became the first European city to offer autonomous rides to the general public, through Uber, but the service still has a human driver for “onboard monitoring”.

On Tuesday, Waymo announced that it plans to launch commercial operations in Munich, Germany, late next year.

Ben Loewenstein, Waymo’s head of policy and government affairs for the UK and Europe, told the Financial Times that the company was currently “working through the safety approval process” with the transport department and was waiting on TfL’s guidance to gain consent.

He added that Waymo was working towards launching a fully autonomous service “by the end of this year” but would not say whether the company would be able to offer paid rides to the general public in that timeframe.

TfL has granted 15 private hire vehicle licences to Ford Mustang Mach-E vehicles equipped with Wayve’s artificial intelligence driving software, as well as surround cameras and radar.

A TfL-licensed private hire driver will sit in the driver’s seat during trips to intervene if necessary, although the software is expected to control the car.

Uber and Wayve plan to launch small-scale commercial pilots with a driver behind the wheel soon.

For its fully driverless launch Wayve plans to switch to a new Nissan Leaf vehicle that is still in production and is due to launch later this year.

Alex Kendall, Wayve’s chief executive, said the company never claimed it would have a fully driverless operation this year.

“I don’t want to put a timeline on it because we want to make sure we pass through [the regulatory process],” he told the FT. “This work is continuing at pace. London is a significant step up in complexity compared to Phoenix or San Francisco.”

Baidu only began testing vehicles in London at the end of last month and has said it plans to launch public rides next year.

Operating taxis without a driver requires approval via a new process, known as an automated passenger services permit, with the government’s Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency. So far, no vehicles have been approved by the DVSA.

fullText:
London and Kyiv in deal to help stop protesters and hostile states targeting military bases and critical infrastructure

AI models trained on Ukrainian battlefield data will be used to stop protesters and foreign states targeting UK defence sites, railways and energy plants under a deal struck between London and Kyiv.

Private companies will also be given access to the vast trove of data from Ukraine’s Avengers AI lab to help build new systems, the first agreement of its kind in the UK.

The scheme will be piloted at a UK defence site, building a model to identify protesters or a hostile-state attack. It uses AI-optimised sensors in buried fibre-optic cables to detect different kinds of movement.

The government has suggested the technology, if proven workable, could be used at airports, prisons, railways and energy infrastructure.

The controversial proscription of the activist group Palestine Action was sparked after the group breached RAF Brize Norton on scooters last June, a highly embarrassing security lapse as a result of which the group was able to deface two military aircraft with spray paint before escaping the site without being detained.

Palestine Action said at the time that it had targeted RAF Voyager aircraft used for transport and refuelling, and that “activists have interrupted Britain’s direct participation in the commission of genocide and war crimes across the Middle East”.

Private companies will be able to access the data once approved by the MoD on a secure platform, though the data sharing is likely to raise alarm among privacy campaigners.

Pilot projects have already been approved with three British AI companies – Sintela, Mind Foundry and Skyral. Sintela, a Bristol-based company that specialises in fibre-optic sensors, recently struck a $35m (£26m) deal with the Trump administration to provide surveillance on the US-Mexico border.

The partnership with the Ukrainian AI lab means new UK security systems can be trained on operational drone datasets, strike mission footage and flight profiles, likely to include Russian sabotage attempts against critical Ukrainian infrastructure.

The cache of four years’ worth of military data contains a far deeper picture than models outside Ukraine have previously been trained on, which had been mostly restricted to open-source data.

The government eventually hopes to use the AI models to predict quickly when infrastructure such as railways, the power grid or military bases might be coming under threat or stress from hostile actors.

That would primarily come from the laying of fibre-optic cables that are able to identify unique movements of people or vehicles around sensitive sites. Ministry of Defence sources said that would specifically include when a site might be targeted by protesters – not just hostile states.

The prime minister, Andy Burnham, said it would be an opportunity for British companies to combine their AI expertise with Ukraine’s battlefield data, which would “accelerate the development of capabilities that not only strengthen our national security but better protect our critical infrastructure and growth in every postcode here at home”.

Other potential projects could include new AI chips to power drones, robotics and automated weapons systems.

Steven Murdoch, a professor of computer science at University College London, said technologies to detect movement from sensors in fibre-optic cables had been around for decades and that it was unclear if data from Ukraine would refine their capabilities.

“I haven’t heard anything that is very convincing, but there is a plausible scenario where they could see something that could be predicted easily and isn’t in any publicly known dataset,” he said.

Ukraine, however, has a lot of other data that may be valuable, especially related to new threats that countries in western Europe might face in the short to medium term.

“What’s valuable is something we’re seeing today which other countries will be worrying about in the future,” Murdoch said. “Anything to do with drones, for example.”

The defence secretary, Wes Streeting, said Ukraine was “pushing the frontier of defence innovation as they bravely resist Putin’s illegal invasion”.

“By combining the UK’s world-leading scientists, engineers and tech companies with Ukraine’s unique battlefield experience and data, we will strengthen both of our nations’ defence and security,” he said.

fullText:
LONDON Aug 25 (Reuters) - Almost half the world's oil comes from countries affected by conflict in 2026, Reuters calculations ‌show, underscoring that current disruptions have eclipsed previous energy crises.

Six months ago, U.S. ‌and Israeli attacks on Iran triggered what has become the largest oil supply crisis on record, with no clear ​end in sight.

At the same time, the Russia-Ukraine war has forced production and refining cuts, including in nearby Kazakhstan this year.

Ongoing conflict in Libya and U.S. restrictions on Venezuelan oil exports at the start of the year have added further strain.

Together, countries affected by those conflicts produced ‌about 45 million barrels per ⁠day of oil based on 2025 output, accounting for more than 43% of global supply, according to Reuters calculations using International Energy Agency data.

The ⁠disruptions have increased the world's reliance on U.S. oil supplies, though that too has occasionally been disrupted by severe weather.

Not all of this year's supply disruptions happened at the same time.

With Saudi Arabia ​re-routing ​oil to the Red Sea and Gulf exporters ​sneaking oil secretly out of the ‌Strait of Hormuz, the current Gulf oil disruption stands at around 5 million to 7 million bpd, according to analysts' estimates.

But risks to total flows remain high, as attacks in the Red Sea and near Egypt's Suez Canal in July demonstrated.

The conflicts in the Gulf and Ukraine have also cut global refining capacity by about a tenth.

Ukraine has targeted much of ‌Russia's refining network, striking plants as far away as ​Omsk, about 2,700 km (1,680 miles) from Ukrainian-held territory.

Russia is ​grappling with fuel shortages and has ​banned gasoline and diesel exports, tightening global fuel markets.

Higher fuel prices have ‌become a key driver of inflation, contributing ​to higher borrowing costs ​and helping to push U.S. debt to a record $40 trillion.

U.S. diesel prices have climbed to record levels despite refiners running at peak capacity.

The IEA has released record volumes ​from emergency stockpiles to ‌help cushion the supply shock. Those releases are now largely complete, even as global ​inventories continue to decline.

title: London Zoo animals hop on scales for weigh-in
description: Kiwi the Capybara is among animals getting their annual health check while data is gathered and shared.
fullText:
Animals at London Zoo are being checked and measured as part of its annual weigh-in day to monitor their health and wellbeing.

Zookeepers will need to coax every bird, reptile, fish and mammal - from the largest rodents in the world to the greenest katydids - to the weighing scale.

Each measurement is added to the Zoological Information Management System (ZIMS), a global database shared with animal carers and conservationists that compares important information on thousands of endangered species.

Many of the zoo's animals are trained to perch on a scale while zookeepers note down their measurements, but others will need to be tempted with a strategic snack.

Although the zoo houses more than 14,000 animals, the keepers will only have time to measure and log the weight of about 400 creatures.

Daniel Simmonds, London Zoo's animal operations manager, said: "Regular weigh-ins help zookeepers track the health of our animals, including invertebrates like the magnolia land snails, the capybaras and Humboldt penguins, and genuinely help us manage the care of these animals, who play a vital role in our global conservation efforts."

Among the animals weighed this year were capybara siblings Kiwi and Gizmo.

Kiwi weighed in at 45kg (7st), while her brother Gizmo tipped the scales at 50.5kg (8st).

While Giant Magnolia Land Snail No 2 weighed a modest 102.5g (3.6oz).

title: London boroughs challenge PM on council tax hikes
description: It follows reforms meaning more money is directed to deprived areas while wealthy areas get less.
fullText:
Three Conservative council leaders in London have written to Andy Burnham, accusing the government of "devolving blame" for council tax hikes.

The leaders of Westminster, Wandsworth and Kensington and Chelsea councils said they were being forced to significantly raise council tax or cut services to plug a hole left by cuts to central government funding.

It follows a reform of council funding, which means more cash is directed to deprived areas.

The Tories want the change reviewed, claiming it will "worsen the lives of local residents across London and the South East". But the government said it was "fixing an outdated system" that benefited wealthy areas while poorer communities lost out.

The reforms made the system "fairer for taxpayers across the country", ministers added.

In a letter, Westminster City Council's Paul Swaddle, Wandsworth Council's Robert Morritt and Kensington and Chelsea Council's Elizabeth Campbell said the government's funding formula "punishes low tax councils".

They said: "If our councils do not impose council tax rises, our communities face considerable cuts in funding for local services.

"This is not just devolving blame, it is devolving council tax rises and government cuts.

"This is fiddled funding, cooked up in Whitehall but leaving town halls to carry the blame."

The three leaders added: "These tax rises are in addition to the new top-up council tax on many homes in our councils – and none of the revenues from this tax penalty will be retained by councils or by the mayor of London.

"There is nothing local about it."

Six councils have been granted two-year "funding realignment powers", which enables them to increase council tax beyond the 5% threshold.

The three Conservative leaders said their councils had been "singled out" for this, alongside the City of London, Hammersmith and Fulham, and Windsor and Maidenhead.

They argued that the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government "assumed massive rises in council tax" in their areas to compensate for cuts to central government funding when publishing its Local Government Finance Settlement.

Backing the council leaders, shadow local government secretary Sir James Cleverly said "true devolution" could not mean imposing high council taxes "from on high".

He said: "London's taxpayers are being forced to pay a Burnham penalty on their council tax.

"The prime minister talks a lot about devolution. But by slashing funding for councils with lower tax rates, he is forcing them to raise taxes drastically or cut services severely."

However, a government spokesperson said: "We're fixing an outdated funding system so funding goes where need is greatest.

"For too long, some of the wealthiest parts of the country have benefited from exceptionally high levels of government support while communities facing greater pressures lost out.

"Our reforms will make the system fairer for taxpayers across the country, while protecting councils through the transition and ensuring no area faces a cliff edge."

The letter comes just weeks after the prime minister announced that English mayors would be allowed to keep a share of the taxes collected in their area.

Burnham said allowing mayors to keep a share of income tax and business rates would help to promote growth "in every postcode".

The council leaders of Westminster, Wandsworth and Kensington and Chelsea claim that "the reverse is happening here".

title: 'If I can make it out, you can too,' says Dyer before UFC fight
description: Shanelle Dyer is using her UFC platform to show young people they can "make it out too" after growing up in a neighbourhood affected by knife crime in west London.
fullText:
Shanelle Dyer's parents always encouraged her to play sports because they were worried about what the alternative could be.

In March, the Londoner introduced herself on the world stage as she knocked out Ravena Oliveira in stunning fashion in the second round on her UFC debut.

The performance follows the best part of a decade in sport, with Dyer eventually finding her home in mixed martial arts after trying ballet, gymnastics and football.

She grew up on a housing estate in west London which was troubled by knife crime and Dyer, now 25, believes she could have gone "down the wrong path" if not for her parents' encouragement.

"Some of it was difficult, especially when you go to school and you find out people in your class got stabbed - some people actually died from my neighbourhood," Dyer told BBC Sport.

"That's heartbreaking because we grew up in the same place, and that could have been me if I went down the wrong path.

"It just happened my parents and family and people around me put me on a great path. It just motivated me, I didn't want to be in that situation, I wanted to be in a better situation."

In 2020, Dyer lost her friend and MMA mentor Jahreau Shepherd when he was stabbed to death by his brother at his 30th birthday party.

Dyer was at the party, but left an hour before the incident happened.

On Saturday in Las Vegas, Dyer's nickname "The Nightmare" will be read out by announcer Bruce Buffer before her strawweight bout against American Elise Reed - an alias she adopted from Shepherd to help keep his memory alive.

"We had the same dream. I remember talking about how we were going to be UFC fighters, UFC champions, walk out to big crowds, that was our dream," said Dyer.

"He didn't get to live out his dream but I can so I'm gonna take him with me.

"Jay is always with me. In my corner, every morning if I don't want to go training I can hear 'get up, you get to live your life - do it'. He's always in the back of my mind."

Dyer started her martial arts career in Muay Thai before transitioning to MMA, in which she has won seven of her eight professional fights, recording five knockouts.

She is hoping for a showing against Reed as impressive as her UFC debut, when she won a performance of the night bonus of $100,000 (£73,000).

The money is a life-changing sum for Dyer, and she has already started giving back to her parents for their part in helping her gravitate towards martial arts when she was younger.

"That bonus is a lot for me. The area I grew up in, you don't see that money in our lifetime, never mind in one night," Dyer explained.

"I'm taking my family to Paris after this fight, it's the first family trip I'm coming to, just to start showing them the bigger picture."

Killings involving a knife or sharp instrument fell by 21% last year, according to figures from police forces in England and Wales.

More than a quarter (28%) of knife-related offences were recorded by the Metropolitan Police in Greater London, although it saw a 17% fall in recorded knife crime compared with the previous year.

Dyer says her success in reaching the UFC proves to young people in troubled neighbourhoods that there is an alternative to gang violence if you "find your niche".

She said: "I have a lot of people on my estate who have found out who I am now. Walking down my estate people are like 'I can't believe you're in the UFC, you actually made it out'.

"Now they want to do the same thing and it's not even all sport, it's different things like music and business. If I can make it out, and I came from the same place as you, you can do exactly the same thing.

"Just surround yourself with the right people. Find great role models and find a place where you belong.

"If you love something put your heart into it. What's the worst thing that could happen?"

title: Day marking victims of terrorist attacks recognises 'my brother's life mattered'
description: The UK's first national day for victims and survivors of terrorism will be held in London on Friday.
fullText:
The UK's first national day for victims and survivors of terrorism is being held in London on Friday where those affected by the violence of the Troubles will be in attendance.

The day aims to recognise people impacted by terrorism including victims and their families, witnesses and the emergency services, as well as raising awareness about specialist support.

For the rest of the UK, these could be terror attacks such as the London Bridge terror attack, the Manchester Arena attack in 2017 or the 7/7 bombings.

But in Northern Ireland, many will be remembering the atrocities of the Troubles, which lasted 30 years and cost the lives of more than 3,500 people.

The government said it introduced the national day for victims and survivors of terrorism following campaigning from victims and survivors for better recognition of their lived experiences.

Claire Hayes is part of a delegation from victims group the South East Fermanagh Foundation travelling from Northern Ireland to England on Friday.

She was 16 when her brother Alan Radford was killed in the Omagh bomb in 1998.

Twenty-nine people, including a woman who was pregnant with twins, were murdered in the Real IRA attack on 15 August 1998.

Hayes called for Stormont to do more to mark the remembrance of those killed in terrorist attacks in Northern Ireland, but said the UK-wide event is a "monumental day".

"It's been very welcomed that Alan is no longer just a statistic, that he is being recognised, that he was a human being, who was here, who was murdered and his life mattered," she told BBC Radio Ulster's Good Morning Ulster.

However, Hayes said has been campaigning for the commemoration to happen for years.

She said there are questions as to why Stormont and its own ministers have not provided them with a day to mark victims locally.

"They like to try and cleanse what has happened in Northern Ireland and I think this is going to be another pushing point for them that they really don't want to," Hayes said.

Hayes also called for more education in Northern Ireland schools about the impact terrorism has on victims.

Tanya Williams-Powell, who's grandfather was abducted and murdered by the IRA more than 50 years ago, said victims are the "most important" when it comes to remembering terrorist attacks.

Thomas Niedermayer was kidnapped from his home in west Belfast two days after Christmas in December 1973.

Powell told the Nolan Show that she felt there is often more interest into why the perpetrator commits a terrorist attack.

"It can almost be glorified. I think it's really important that we teach history honestly," said Williams-Powell.

"The victims are the most important and we need to make sure as much as we can that young people don't glorify it and continue the violence."

Speaking ahead of the first national day for victims and survivors of terrorism Secretary of State Chris Bryant said "few places have borne more pain than in Northern Ireland".

"I'm amazed and inspired by the fortitude and grace so many victims, survivors, and bereaved families have shown over the years, often suffering in silence," he said.

"As we stand with the victims and survivors of terrorism we commit ourselves anew to keep people safe and remember the past with honesty."

The chosen date for the national day of 21 August coincides with the UN International Day of Remembrance and Tribute to the Victims of Terrorism, which began in 2017.

While the UK event will take place in London for its debut year, the Home Office has said people across the country can mark it at home by observing a moment of reflection and sharing posts about the day on social media.

title: Proposed London datacentre will have annual carbon footprint of 27,000 flights to New York
description:
Exclusive: Planning documents show datacentre in North Ockendon would be incompatible with UK net zero targets

fullText:
Exclusive: Planning documents show datacentre in North Ockendon would be incompatible with UK net zero targets

A “hyperscale” datacentre in outer London would generate more than 1m tonnes of carbon dioxide a year, equivalent to the carbon footprint of 27,000 flights from London to New York, planning documents show.

The East Havering Data Centre Campus (EHDCC) in North Ockendon would be one of the largest datacentres in Europe if approved by Havering council, using 218 hectares of green belt to run servers and data storage systems for AI and cloud computing. Its developer, Digital Reef, has described the scheme as “a unique opportunity to create a sustainable datacentre campus of the future”.

But in the planning application, Digital Reef says the £14.7bn project “does not align with a science-based 1.5C compatible trajectory and achieving net zero by 2050”. Documents estimate the development would generate more than 72m tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO₂e) over its projected 60-year lifespan – 1.2m tonnes annually once fully operational.

Guardian analysis of planning documents for the dozens of proposed datacentres in the UK shows that the EHDCC has the highest projected carbon emissions disclosed by a developer.

Donald Campbell, advocacy director at the tech justice nonprofit Foxglove, said the EHDCC’s projected emissions were “staggering”.

“It’s a big threat to the ability to decarbonise in the UK,” he said. “It’s also going to be a big drain on important resources that are needed by homes and other businesses.”

According to Ofgem, the average UK household electricity consumption is 2,500 kWh per year. Digital Reef said in its proposal that at a “likely” 50% load, the campus would consume 2.65bn kWh per year of electricity, equivalent to the demand of more than 1m UK households.

The campus would be powered primarily by a huge 600MVA connection to the National Grid via the nearby Warley substation. Because the existing site does not have sufficient capacity, major upgrades are planned, including a new 400kV National Grid substation and a new 132kV UK Power Networks facility on adjacent land, with the full connection expected by 2033.

The 1.2m tonnes of CO₂e the EHDCC expects to emit would amount to 26,795 long-haul flights from London Heathrow to New York’s John F Kennedy international airport, according to the UN’s International Civil Aviation Organization’s carbon calculator.

North Ockendon Residents Association said the development would be a “massacre” of green belt land. “It’s crop-producing farmland, in an age when we are threatened by security, it’s the loss of wildlife habitats, and there’s the pollution cost, which everyone seems to brush under the carpet,” a group spokesperson said.

The scale of datacentre emissions raises questions over how Britain’s rapid expansion of AI infrastructure can be reconciled with the government’s legally binding climate targets.

The government designated datacentres as “critical national infrastructure” in 2024, putting the tech developments on an equal footing with water, energy and emergency services systems.

In January, planning legislation was amended so datacentre developers were able to apply as nationally significant infrastructure projects, meaning they were able to largely bypass the local authority planning procedure and seek approval directly from government.

Neso, Britain’s grid operator, has warned MPs that datacentre developers have requested 72.8GW of electricity connections by 2039 – a “huge step change for the sector” and nearly 60% more than the UK’s peak power demand last year – in a surge driven by the race to build AI and hyperscale infrastructure.

The government said last year the now disbanded department for science, innovation and technology (DSIT) would produce a national policy statement for the sector, but it has not yet been published.

Campbell said: “The government needs to be taking concrete steps to make sure that the public and the environment aren’t left to carry the social environmental costs of the datacentres. These datacentres are ultimately going to be serving the wealthiest companies in the world – so they need to be required to carry that cost.”

Planning documents said that where the zero-carbon target cannot be met on site, “any shortfall would be provided through a cash in lieu contribution to the borough’s carbon offset fund”. The developer estimates that payment at about £77.6m.

Campbell said datacentre developers should at a minimum be required to build enough additional renewable generation and storage to supply their facilities. “That’s the only way of really ensuring that it’s not going to add to carbon emissions,” he said. “They shouldn’t just plug into the grid and drain the power that everyone else needs.”

The first round of consultation on the EHDCC closed in April. A revised proposal reflecting any accepted changes is expected to be published for a further public consultation in the autumn.

Councillor Keith Prince, Reform UK leader of Havering council, said that as a decision on EHDCC is made by the local planning authority, it would be “wrong” to comment until that decision was made.

Digital Reef did not respond to request for comment.

title: Would Marmoush joining Tottenham be a masterstroke or risk?
description: Tottenham are working on a deal for Omar Marmoush, but what could the Man City forward bring to the north London team?
fullText:
Tottenham are looking to sign Manchester City forward Omar Marmoush, with talks between the clubs progressing.

No agreement has yet been reached, but the Egypt international could become the latest addition to Roberto De Zerbi's squad, with the north London club's summer spending looking set to exceed £300m.

Spurs have already spent £229.5m on centre-back Jan Paul van Hecke and midfielders Sandro Tonali and Mateus Fernandes.

And on Friday it was announced that they have agreed a £75m deal to sign Manchester City winger Savinho as they look to strengthen their attack.

Spurs forward Dominic Solanke has endured injury problems over the past 18 months, while team-mate Richarlison has entered the final year of his contract.

Marmoush's influence at City has diminished but the numbers suggest Tottenham would be getting a forward whose skillset differs considerably from their existing options.

Spurs in talks to sign Man City's Savinho and Marmoush

Joining Eintracht Frankfurt in May 2023 on a free transfer from Wolfsburg, the then 24-year-old Marmoush found form in his first season with the German side scoring 17 times across all competitions.

He then scored 15 Bundesliga goals from 8.9 expected goals (xG) during the first half of 2024-25, while registering nine assists in 17 league appearances. Across all competitions before leaving Germany, he had 20 goals and 13 assists in 26 games.

Set-pieces were another notable part of his game. Marmoush became the first player in Europe's top five leagues since Lionel Messi in 2019 to score directly from a free-kick in three consecutive competitive matches. Manchester City then paid £59m for him in January 2025.

The early signs were encouraging. Marmoush scored his first career hat-trick against Newcastle, struck the winner in City's FA Cup quarter-final at Bournemouth and then scored from long range against the same opponents in the Premier League. It was judged to be the goal of the season.

But there were difficult moments too.

With City trailing Crystal Palace in the 2025 FA Cup final, Erling Haaland handed Marmoush the ball for a penalty. His effort was saved by Dean Henderson as City went on to lose at Wembley.

Former Manchester City defender Nedum Onuoha does not believe that moment should define Marmoush's spell at the club.

"When I see Marmoush, I don't see the penalty miss," Onuoha told BBC Sport. "I see the strength he has with some of the runs he makes in behind."

Marmoush has scored 16 goals in 62 appearances in all competitions for City since arriving from Frankfurt.

Eight of those came in 36 appearances in 2025-26, but his Premier League involvement fell considerably.

He started only eight league games and played around 700 minutes, fewer than he managed after joining midway through the prior campaign.

His league return was three goals and three assists, with his 3.53 expected goals figure close to his actual scoring output. The issue was therefore not simply finishing.

Marmoush found himself competing for minutes in a side built around Haaland, while City further strengthened their attacking options.

"All the positions Marmoush could play are being filled by people who are specialists in those roles," said Onuoha. "Haaland is essentially always going to be the number nine, while City also regularly play with number 10s and Guardiola likes his wingers to stay wide."

Marmoush is primarily a number nine, but he has rarely been confined to one role across the front line.

At Frankfurt he was used predominantly through the middle but also appeared as a second striker and from the left. City have followed a similar pattern, using him mainly as a central attacker while also deploying him from the flank and just behind another forward.

That flexibility could suit De Zerbi. His teams have often relied on forwards changing positions, dropping towards the ball and then attacking the space created when opponents are drawn out. Marmoush is comfortable doing both.

Onuoha sees the Egyptian as most dangerous when he is able to threaten the space beyond the defence.

"As much as he is good dropping towards the ball, I think he is better when he plays on the shoulder," he said. "He needs to be in a team that will constantly play balls in behind and force the opposition to run back towards their own goal. That's when you see a better version of Marmoush."

Opta's Premier League numbers from last season show he averaged 11.46 runs in behind per 90 minutes, almost identical to Solanke's 11.61 and ahead of Richarlison's 10.03. But he also offered considerably more with the ball.

Marmoush averaged 5.67 progressive carries per 90 minutes, compared with 3.24 for Solanke and 2.48 for Richarlison.

He also led both Tottenham forwards for shots, chances created, successful take-ons and touches in the opposition penalty area.

He had 3.86 shots per 90 minutes compared with 2.81 for Richarlison and 1.80 for Solanke, while Marmoush created 1.55 chances against 0.92 and 0.54 respectively.

He also produced 0.77 goals and assists per game, ahead of Richarlison's 0.69 and Solanke's 0.27.

The sample is smaller because of his limited league minutes, but the profile is clear.

Marmoush is more inclined to take opponents on and manufacture shooting opportunities for himself than Spurs' existing central forwards.

That could make him particularly useful when opponents sit deep and deny Tottenham the space to attack directly. Onuoha feels De Zerbi's style could suit him better.

"Sometimes the fit can simply be better," he said. "Marmoush's ability to run in behind and link the play could be huge assets for Spurs. They won't be shy about playing those passes into him and forcing opponents on to the back foot."

Marmoush would not necessarily have to replace Solanke.

His experience playing off another attacker creates the possibility of using the pair together, with Solanke occupying central defenders while Marmoush moves into wider areas or drops between the lines.

That may be particularly attractive to De Zerbi because Marmoush can also accelerate into the spaces opened when Tottenham play through an opposition press.

"Solanke is different to Marmoush. He's got more of a physical presence," said Onuoha. "I could see the goalkeeper playing a flat ball into Solanke, Marmoush coming underneath him to receive it, and that becoming the start of the attack.

"The two of them could complement each other. Playing in a front two might bring out more of Marmoush's strengths."

title: Why the Pacers picked streaming service DAZN as regional broadcast partner
description: The Pacers announced on Thursday morning that they will be partnering with DAZN, a global sports streaming service based in London, as its TV partner.
fullText:
The Pacers' regional sports television rights have been in some form of limbo for more than three years since one broadcast partner went bankrupt and then the company that emerged in its place quickly found itself unable to make its rights payments.

So this offseason, after Main Street Sports Group -- the owner of the FanDuel Sports Network -- announced that it was winding down operations, the Pacers embarked on a search for a new regional broadcast partner and landed on one that takes a much different approach than the old model. This one does not have a traditional broadcast or cable channel and markets directly to the consumer, but it comes at a price.

The Pacers announced Thursday morning that they have entered into an agreement with the United Kingdom-based sports streaming company DAZN (pronounced Da-Zone) as its exclusive regional broadcast partner. Pacers fans who want to watch games on DAZN would have to download the company's streaming app, which could be done on any internet-connected devices including smart phones, laptops and smart televisions, but DAZN does not have a presence on any cable or satellite packages. The team announced that there will be 22 regular season games available for free on the DAZN app and that 15 of those games would also be expected to available on a local over-the-air broadcast partner. A local partner has not yet been chosen but Pacers executives say they expect to make that choice sometime in the next few weeks before the season starts.

Access to the rest of the games would require a season pass. Full price for the pass is $119.99 for the season, but fans who sign up before Oct. 15 can purchase an early-bird season pass for $59.99. A monthly pass will also be available for $19.99 per month. Season ticket holders will receive a free season pass. There will be a landing page on the DAZN app that will house all of Pacers content where fans will be directed to for subscription.

The Pacers will be in charge of the actual production of the broadcasts, meaning the announcers will remain the same. Chris Denari will be the play-by-play announcer for the 21st consecutive season, Quinn Buckner will be the color analyst, Jeremiah Johnson will be the sideline reporter and Eddie Gill will assist Johnson on the pregame, halftime and postgame shows while also maintaining his role as radio color analyst with Mark Boyle on play-by-play.

Pacers Sports and Entertainment CEO Mel Raines told reporters in an embargoed briefing Wednesday that the contract is a five-year deal, and though it gives the Pacers the opportunity to opt out in the future if the NBA puts together a regional sports television hub as it has been exploring, they could maintain the deal if the NBA and DAZN partner together on the hub, which is a possibility.

DAZN will be partnering with several of the 13 NBA teams whose rights became available when Main Street Sports Group effectively went under. The company already announced a partnership with the Minnesota Timberwolves and Raines indicated there will be more to come.

"When we were looking at partners -- and I should say, we probably talked to a dozen different options across the board -- one of the things we wanted to do was find somebody who we thought could be what the league refers to as their aggregated solution where you would aggregate all the teams," Raines said. "DAZN is certainly a top potential partner and that's been in the news. They were the only partner we were talking to who was going to potentially continue on. We are looking at this as a long-term partnership. It's a five-year deal, but ... the league required all the teams to have a potential out if there was an aggregated solution. We also don't have to necessarily opt into that. We're looking at this as we are happily in a five-year marriage with DAZN and hope the fans jump on board and love the service as much as we do."

Raines and Pacers Sports and Entertainment executive vice president and chief commercial officer Joey Graziano, who also met with the media Wednesday, said they tried to keep fans first and foremost in their thoughts when they were making their decision. They noted, however, that it's harder to please the entire fanbase now that sports and entertainment consumption have become so fragmented.

Graziano said that in their preparation, the Pacers learned that in 2010, almost 88% of households in the Pacers' designated market area had access to paid -- i.e. cable and satellite-- television. In 2026, that number has fallen to around 30%. The consistent trend of cord-cutting is a big reason why Diamond Sports Group -- which operated the Bally Sports Networks -- filed Chapter 11 bankruptcy in 2023 and the Main Street Sports Group that ran the Fan Duel Sports Networks had to effectively go out of business at the end of the 2025-26 NBA season. Graziano said that indicated that the Pacers had to pursue a digital-first strategy and market to fans through the internet rather than traditional linear television.

"We needed a solution that our fans could be able to access," Graziano said. "The way most of us are accessing our lives are via the internet in some way, having something that felt accessible across a variety of different modes and channels. That means your phone. That also may mean the tablet that you have. It may mean your gaming console. It may mean your smart television. We wanted something that would meet our fans exactly where they are as they're traveling in their busy lives."

Of course, not all of the Pacers' fans are in the same place and they know they'll have to deal with a portion of the fanbase that will not be pleased with this move. Their could be older fans without home access to the internet or fans who are already paying for television access who will be displeased to be asked to pay money for another subscription. The best the Pacers can do in that case, they noted, is try to be as accessible as possible in trying to guide those fans toward a new experience.

"Of course we're concerned about it," Graziano said. "We're concerned about all of our fans and we're going to be incredibly responsive to any concerns that come about for that. ... We've got to think about how we make sure those fans are able to We have an entire marketing and digital team who is hyper focused on fan feedback and we will be responsive to fan's concerns about their ability to access. That's an important part of our thought of how do you bring this together. There certainly will be some fans that may represent some challenges and as an organization we will address them."

Raines noted that the Pacers do not have access to some over-the-air opportunities that are available to others. Several teams, including the Bucks, Magic and Heat, have announced that they will broadcast all of their games on free over-the-air television this season. Raines said those teams were able to take advantage of effectively dead channels on their local packages that aren't available in the Indianapolis area.

"Some markets had the opportunity with a Scripps or a Grey to have an empty channel that is already bought into the lower tier of Comcast or Spectrum or DirecTV or Dish," Raines said. "That's not available in our market right now. As you know there's been a lot of consolidation. Unfortunately we didn't have that opportunity."

They also couldn't expect to ask a local broadcast affiliate of one of the big four national networks -- ABC, CBS, NBC and FOX -- to commit to showing all of the games that will not be broadcast nationally. The Pacers will appear on some form of national broadcast 11 times in their 82 regular season games -- once on ESPN, once on NBC, four times on Amazon Prime and five times on Peacock. Even getting 15 games over the air as they plan to, Raines said, is ambitious.

"They can't clear 71 games," Raines said. "They have network programming that they can't pre-empt 71 times. To get 15 at their peak season is difficult to be honest. If it was easy we'd be telling you who it was today. They have to navigate being able to pre-empt broadcast TV. There really isn't a single solution out there that hits 100% of the fans anymore or I'd tell you those 13 teams -- us being one of them -- would have already done that deal six months ago. That's what we're trying to do and I think our best shot at it is a partner like this."

DAZN has extensive experience with this situation, especially overseas, and the company was aggressive in courting the 13 teams that had partnered with Main Street. Raines said DAZN was the only potential partner that wanted to come to Indiana for an in-person meeting. Zander Berlinksi, DAZN's senior vice president of strategy and business development, also attended Wednesday's press briefing.

According to the press release announcing the partnership, DAZN streams more than 140,000 live events annually and is available in more than 200 markets worldwide. The United States overall market accounts for a relatively small percentage of its business, but it partners with some of the biggest sports leagues in Europe and Japan, and also serves as a global distributor for U.S. sports leagues. Berlinski said DAZN owns the exclusive rights to Italy's Serie A soccer league and Spain's La Liga as well as much of the domestic baseball in Japan. It also, according to Berlinski, is the largest partner for the NFL internationally outside of the U.S. and China as it platforms NFL Game Pass internationally.

"Over the last 10 years, we've built a tremendous tech platform that is powered by 2,000-plus engineers that is purpose-built for sports," Berlinski said, "and has experienced working with teams and leagues across the world to help grow audiences."

Dustin Dopirak covers the Pacers all season. Get more coverage on IndyStarTV and with the Pacers Insider newsletter.

fullText:
Patrons at two of the chain’s London pubs were all for Tim Martin’s ban on playing music or taking calls on speaker

The terrace of the Moon Under Water Wetherspoons pub in Leicester Square was full of people enjoying the warm weather and chatting between tables – without a TikTok video or speakerphone call in earshot.

At Wetherspoons, the convivial atmosphere can no longer be punctuated by rude customers taking phone calls on blast, or playing videos without headphones after Tim Martin, the owner of the pub chain, banned both actions on his premises.

Gary and Mark, two brothers who were catching up over pints, both thought anyone playing loud sounds in the pub should be barred.

“There is no way anyone should be allowed to be obnoxious enough to have their phone on loud. Why should people choose to play music that I don’t like and that other people around them don’t like?” asked Mark. “I listen to music with headphone on, in a private way.”

But Gary pointed out: “First they didn’t used to allow televisions in Wetherspoons but now they have TVs with the sound on. External noise is becoming part of the pub.”

Abdslam Elidrisi, 65, who was puffing on a cigar with a glass of white wine while people-watching, also welcomed the move.

“I come here because I am a member of a film club nearby and they don’t let me smoke my cigar, so I visit here to smoke it and watch the world go by,” he said, “Music is a personal thing, so I agree with Mr Martin. You can’t impose it on other people. Loud phone calls are the same thing. I don’t want to hear about your personal life – unless you are having a conversation with me about it!”

The company announced on Tuesday it had introduced the ban across its 792 pubs, saying sound from smartphones and tablets had become an “increasing problem in recent years”.

“In a world dominated by other people’s music and amplified sound, Wetherspoon pubs are an oasis of tranquillity and contemplation,” Martin said. “We are kindly asking phone users to pipe down.”

The pub company has recently been clamping down on some modern behaviours – including banning the use of Meta’s “spy glasses” to record inside pubs. The glasses contain very small cameras that enable the wearer to discreetly film.

Lily, 21, and Avril, 22, both students, agreed it was antisocial and inconsiderate to play video and phone calls out loud in the pub, but said they weren’t regularly troubled by it when visiting Wetherspoons for chicken burgers and spritzes. “I’ve seen it on the train,” Avril said.

Trev and John, who work laying cables for telecoms, were enjoying a quiet after-work pint. “I think it’s a great idea,” said Trev. “People have loud speakerphone conversations right next to you and you can’t enjoy your pint. In a pub, you don’t want that. I take my phone calls outside.”

Over at the Montagu Pyke Wetherspoons near Tottenham Court Road in central London, not everyone had got the memo.

“Someone was doing it just now, taking a loud call on speakerphone; it annoys me and it is inconsiderate,” said Mel Burton, 41, who works in the packaging industry and had just finished a late pub lunch.

Her colleague Sam Reid, 48, was supportive of the ban. “It does piss me off when people play music out of their phones,” he said. “I don’t want to hear someone else’s music.”

The manager of the Montagu Pyke said she had had to tell people to turn off the sound on their phones on a number of occasions. “It annoys me, it annoys other customers. I have to ask them to stop,” she said. “If it’s been banned by the whole company, it means it must be an issue across the different Wetherspoons. Some people understand when we ask them to turn off the noise – others are looking for a fight.”

Holly and Eleanor, both 18, were enjoying a meal after a day of shopping in central London, having come down from Darlington on the train. “We actually saw this happening on the train this morning, someone was on their phone playing music out loud,” said Holly.

“I agree with banning it in pubs, it’s loud and annoying, it should be banned on the train as well,” Eleanor added.

The London mayor, Sadiq Khan, started a campaign last year encouraging people to use headphones when playing music on the city’s transport network.

title: 'Rest in Power': Thousands gather in London for vigil honouring academic Arday
description: Thousands attended a vigil in central London on Monday for Jason Arday, a former University of Cambridge sociology professor who was found dead on Friday
fullText:
LONDON, Aug 17 (Reuters) - Thousands attended a vigil in central London on Monday for Jason Arday, a former University of Cambridge sociology professor who was found dead on Friday ‌after weeks of intense scrutiny over accusations of plagiarism and other claims.

Arday, once hailed as Cambridge's ‌youngest Black professor, resigned on August 5 after a former researcher accused him of plagiarism in his PhD thesis. British Prime Minister Andy ​Burnham described his death as "a tragedy on so many levels."

Arday denied the allegation but acknowledged making mistakes.

The plagiarism allegations drew huge media interest, leading to questions about other elements of his life, including claims he made about his career, personal life and medical conditions.

His family said on Friday that he had been the victim of misinformation and harassment.

Campaign ‌group Stand up to Racism organised Monday's ⁠vigil to honour Arday. People carried flowers and placards — some reading "Rest In Power Professor Jason Arday" — as they gathered in Trafalgar Square, a historic centre for protest in the ⁠British capital.

Before his death, Arday had become a focal point for often polarising commentary about the state of British society, including on race, academic rigour, police interference and media intrusion.

Cambridge University pledged on Wednesday to investigate the ​circumstances ​of his appointment and his academic work.

Critics have argued the ​university was so keen to hire a ‌Black academic that it failed to check Arday's credentials sufficiently and did not respond appropriately when the plagiarism claims emerged.

On Monday, university Chancellor Chris Smith defended the university's approach.

"I do believe it is possible to hold to two principles at the same time: to believe in the importance of academic integrity, and where criticisms of plagiarism arise, about any academic, whoever they are, ensure that they are rigorously investigated," he told the BBC.

"And also to ‌refuse to join in a racist feeding frenzy over a ​particular academic."

Britain's Metropolitan Police apologised to a journalist for investigating a ​complaint against the journalist after he contacted Arday ​for comment on the plagiarism accusations a year before the story was made public.

The ‌scrutiny once those accusations were published extended to ​questioning Arday's accounts of his ​childhood struggles with autism and his sporting achievements — including that he ran 30 marathons in 35 days.

"He was being subjected to relentless scrutiny, including ridicule, discrediting absolutely every detail of his life," Simon Baron-Cohen, ​a Cambridge professor and supporter of ‌Arday, told BBC radio on Saturday.

He said Arday was a vulnerable person since childhood and deserved ​safeguarding and support, adding investigations into the case should assign accountability "at lots of levels".

title: Jason Arday, ex-Cambridge professor at centre of plagiarism row, found dead
description: His family said it was "in shock to have lost this amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son" after the academic was found dead in London on Friday.
fullText:
Jason Arday, the former University of Cambridge professor at the centre of a plagiarism row, has been found dead.

Emergency services said a man was found "unresponsive" at an address in Battersea, south London, on Friday afternoon.

Arday resigned as a Cambridge professor of sociology of education last week after allegations of plagiarism and questions about some of his achievements. He had denied the claims.

Arday's family said in a statement that they were "in shock to have lost this amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son".

They added: "The campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason, who was a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone."

Earlier on Friday, police officers were called to an address in Battersea by the London Ambulance Service.

In a statement, the Metropolitan Police said: "At this time his death is being treated as unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious."

Cambridge University vice-chancellor Prof Deborah Prentice said: "We are desperately saddened to hear this tragic news."

"Our heartfelt sympathies go to Jason Arday's family and friends at this incredibly difficult time," she said.

Education Secretary Lucy Powell said she was "deeply shocked and saddened" to hear about the death and she urged people to "remember there are real people with loved ones involved".

Arday, 41, had denied any plagiarism - but admitted errors in his work - and last week said the recent controversy about his work had led to "an unrelenting level of public scrutiny and personal attack".

The row first erupted after another academic - self-defined "race realist" Nathan Cofnas, who was sacked from his Cambridge role in 2024 - said he found numerous instances of plagiarism in the professor's work.

Arday said some errors in his early academic work arose because of his autism, as he relied on using mimicry to make sense of information. Similar scrutiny would find similar errors in work by other academics, he said.

"We're talking about academia here. I didn't murder somebody. I think the cruelty that I've experienced and the positioning of me as this kind of liar and fantasist is totally unacceptable," he told the Times newspaper earlier this month.

Arday's appointment as Cambridge's youngest ever black professor at the age of 37 in 2023 was hailed at the time as a progressive moment.

Announcing his resignation last week, Arday said the "personal cost" of the scrutiny of him had become "too great".

He said: "While criticism is an inevitable part of academic life, what I have experienced has gone far beyond scholarly disagreement.

"The relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love."

He stressed that his resignation should not "be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me".

Cambridge initially said claims of plagiarism regarding Arday's thesis and some journal publications had been investigated by Liverpool John Moores University (LJMU) and the journals in question.

LJMU - which awarded Arday his PhD in 2015 - concluded that he had not plagiarised work.

Earlier this week, Cambridge announced an independent investigation into his appointment.

In a letter to university staff at the time, Prof Prentice said: "I fully understand the concerns being raised across the university and well beyond it, regarding Jason Arday's appointment and I share them...

"That investigation, as you say, should be thorough and transparent, and will be carried out independently by senior academics from within and beyond Cambridge."

Cambridge celebrated Arday's appointment as a young black professor, one of a tiny and visible majority in academia. Only one per cent of professors in UK universities are black, making each appointment hugely significant.

The university will have to answer bigger questions including about its duty of care after it put him into a very prominent position.

It may also find itself the lightning rod for anger from several different quarters, including those who feel Arday was persecuted publicly and those who question whether he should ever have been appointed.

Jolyon Maugham from campaign group Good Law Project said Arday's death was "a tragedy".

"I do not understand what the public interest was in continuing to hound him after he resigned as a professor and I do not understand what risk assessments media outlets did," Maugham added.

Speaking to BBC Newsnight, Professor of Black Studies Kehinde Andrews and friend of Arday described him as "very down" after resigning from Cambridge.

"He was very upset. He felt that there was no way out. He effectively wasn't leaving the house. He had lost a lost of weight," Andrews said.

"There should be a wakeup call to just how bad black academics actually have it in academia," he added.

Labour MP Bell Ribeiro-Addy told the programme "the idea that an academic would be dragged through this amount of media scrutiny is unheard of".

Arday originally worked as a PE teacher before earning his doctorate at LJMU and going on to become an associate professor at Durham University and professor of sociology of education at the University of Glasgow.

Glasgow university also announced a review into Arday's previous academic work.

When news of his death emerged, the university said in a statement it was "shocked and saddened" by the death of a former colleague.

"Our thoughts and deepest sympathies are with his friends and family at this desperately sad time," it added.

Durham University, another of Arday's former employers, described him as "a kind and warm person, who actively sought to promote opportunities for PhD students".

Last weekend, Arday cancelled an event promoting his memoir.

Publisher Simon & Schuster previously said that the book, Great And Unfortunate Things, would be published in the UK on 27 August. It was released in the US earlier this week.

The book tells the story of his life from being non-verbal until the age of 11 and unable to read or write until 18, then going through a series of "improbable triumphs and heartbreaking setbacks", before being appointed professor of sociology of education at Cambridge.

title: Fire eliminated after narrow defeat by Spirit
description: Welsh Fire are eliminated from The Hundred as they suffer a six-run defeat by London Spirit in their final group phase match in Cardiff.
fullText:
The Hundred men's competition, Sophia Gardens

London Spirit 131-8 (100 balls): Bairstow 34 (19); Jansen 2-16

Welsh Fire 125-7 (100 balls): Cox 44 (28); Willey 3-20

Welsh Fire were eliminated from The Hundred as they suffered a six-run defeat by London Spirit in their final group phase match in Cardiff.

Fire finished their campaign four points behind Manchester Super Giants and Sunrisers Leeds, who are second and third respectively, with four wins from eight matches.

MI London, who are fourth, can still qualify for the Eliminator at the expense of Sunrisers if they defeat Birmingham Phoenix by a significant margin today.

Heading into their final fixture, the Welsh side's hopes of progressing were effectively over because of their net run-rate of -1.001, and they were handed a target of 132 by Spirit to chase down.

Fire looked on course for a routine win as Joe Root and Jordan Cox produced a 47-run stand to take them to 90-2.

Root departed for a run-a-ball 31 but Cox accelerated to reach 44 from 28 balls, leaving his side needing 15 runs to win from eight balls with six wickets in hand.

But Fire then lost Tom Kohler-Cadmore and Rachin Ravindra in quick succession, with Marco Jansen needing a six from the final ball to level the score.

Jansen slapped David Willey over midwicket hoping to clear the rope but was caught by Jamie Overton at deep as they finished narrowly short.

Sent out to bat first, Spirit never fully gained momentum as the Fire bowlers produced a disciplined display to restrict the visitors to 131-8 in Cardiff.

Jonny Bairstow's 34 from 19 balls provided the early impetus for Spirit while James Coles and Jamie Overton also added 29 and 21 respectively.

But none were able to convert their starts into a substantial innings as Chris Woakes and Jansen picked up two wickets apiece.

Spirit ended their campaign seventh in the table with three wins.

Today is the last day of the group phase so the competition takes a very brief break on Thursday before the knockouts start on Friday.

Both the men's and women's Eliminator matches will take place at The Oval with Sunrisers Leeds facing Southern Brave in the women's contest from 14:15 BST.

Manchester Super Giants will be in the men's Eliminator from 18:00 with their opponent still to be determined.

The finals at Lord's follow on Sunday with Trent Rockets men's and women's sides awaiting the winners of the Eliminators.

title: Perry fifty takes Phoenix to victory over MI London
description: Ellyse Perry hits a superb 62 not out to lead Birmingham Phoenix to a five-wicket victory over MI London in The Hundred.
fullText:
The Hundred women's competition, Edgbaston

MI London 120-6 (100 balls): Henry 42 (33); Gray 2-29

Birmingham Phoenix 121-5 (94 balls): Perry 62* (39); Gordon 2-20

Birmingham Phoenix won by five wickets

Ellyse Perry hit a superb unbeaten half-century to lead Birmingham Phoenix to a five-wicket victory over MI London in The Hundred.

The Australia great finished on 62 not out from 39 balls as Phoenix, set 121 to win, got over the line with six balls to spare at Edgbaston.

It is just a second win of a difficult campaign for Phoenix but one that ensures they leapfrog MI London and avoid finishing bottom of the women's table.

Having opted to chase, Phoenix were quickly on top as they reduced MI London to 29-3 and then 47-4, before a 57-run stand between West Indies' Chinelle Henry and captain Hollie Armitage helped get the visitors up to 120-6.

It looked like being enough as Phoenix lost Alice Capsey and Emma Lamb in quick succession to slip to 48-4 in reply.

But Perry remained and the 35-year-old showed all of her class and experience to control the chase from there.

Fatima Sana provided the support Perry needed, scoring 36 from 32 in a fifth-wicket partnership of 66.

The Pakistan skipper couldn't quite see it through and it was left to Perry, who hit seven fours and two sixes in a classy knock, to finish the job - drilling a four through mid-off to level the scores before winning it with a delicate scoop.

fullText:
With so much attention on youth the last few weeks, don't overlook Anna Huang. She made it through Ladies European Tour qualifying at age 16, and the Canadian has not missed a beat.

Huang was caught in a duel with Charley Hull on Sunday in the PIF London and held her nerve. Hull four-putted for double bogey on the 17th hole and Huang closed with an eagle to win by two. The 17-year-old now has four LET victories in the last 11 months.

When she won in Morocco in May, Huang became the youngest player with three LET wins, surpassing records previously held by Lydia Ko.

Huang's fourth victory allowed her to break into the top 50 in the women's world ranking at No. 43, and she moved to No. 2 behind Casandra Alexander on the tour's Order of Merit.

title: Hull lets late lead slip as Huang, 17, wins again
description: England's Charley Hull lets slip a one-shot lead with two holes to play at the PIF London Championship as 17-year-old Anna Huang wins her fourth event on the Ladies' European Tour.
fullText:
-22 A Huang (Can); -20 C Hull (Eng); -17 S Tan (Sin); -15 P Tavatanakit (Tha), -14 K Bennett (Aus)

Selected others: -12 A Hewson (Eng); -11 L Hall (Wal); -10 G Hall (Eng), A Donegan (Ire)

England's Charley Hull let slip a one-shot lead with two holes to play at the PIF London Championship as 17-year-old Anna Huang won her fourth Ladies' European Tour (LET) event.

The 30-year-old Hull was on course for her 10th professional title and sixth LET success, but four-putted the penultimate hole for a double bogey, while Huang eagled the last to win by two shots.

"That was probably the most thrilling round of golf of my life, that was crazy, I'm just so shocked," the Canadian told the LET website.

"I knew coming down three tough holes was not easy and I tried to focus on each shot because anything can happen in golf and I stayed in my own lane.

"I can't believe I made another eagle. I focused on the putt and made a good stroke, and it went in.

"Charley is such a phenomenal player and playing with her in the past two days in the final group has been really cool. The crowds have been cheering really loud, so it was really fun to be part of the last group."

The tournament took place at Centurion Club, near St Albans, and Huang led after the first round with a six-under round of 67.

Hull's first round on Thursday had been a one-over 74, but she catapulted herself into contention with an 11-under 62 on Friday to equal the lowest round in LET history and break the course record at the Centurion Club.

Huang's best round came on Saturday with an eight-under 65 and she began the last round with a three-stroke advantage.

Birdies on the sixth, ninth, 13th, 15th and 16th took Hull into the lead by one shot, but that disappointing double-bogey five on the par-three 17th handed the advantage back to Huang and she finished in style.

Hull, who birdied the last for a 69, finished on 20 under to be three clear of Singapore's Shannon Tan, with Thailand's Patty Tavatanakit fourth on 15 under.

title: Unmasking London City's Spanish superstar
description: Alexia Putellas' arrival at London City Lionesses was the biggest transfer in WSL history - but who is the person behind the global stardom?
fullText:
There is not a single empty seat as Alexia Putellas walks into a room at a hotel in Maidstone ready to speak to the English media for the first time.

"Woah," the two-time Ballon d'Or winner says as she opens the door and sees all the journalists looking in her direction, eager to finally meet her.

You would think that somebody who is referred to as 'La Reina' - the queen - in Spain is used to that kind of attention.

She is considered one of the greatest players of her generation, captained Barcelona to a fourth Women's Champions League title in May and is a World Cup winner with Spain.

But Putellas, who signed for London City Lionesses this summer in what is being touted as the biggest signing in WSL history, is embarking on a different journey with her new club that brings all the stresses and uncertainties anyone would face.

She sat down with the BBC's Women's Football Weekly podcast and addressed media in a press conference that helped unmask the global superstar.

From Barcelona to Bromley: Inside Putellas' move to LCL

Putellas was born in a municipality of Catalonia called Mollet del Valles in the province of Barcelona, and regularly watched games at Nou Camp as a child.

Former Spain and Barcelona star Andres Iniesta was an inspiration to her, while she has also named Brazilian duo Rivaldo and Ronaldinho as players she idolised.

Putellas attended summer football camps ran by Xavi and played for local side CE Sabadell as a child.

She spent a year at La Masia, Barcelona's famous youth academy, but had to leave when her girls team was disbanded.

After spells at Espanyol and Levante, she eventually returned to Barca in 2012 - the start of an incredible 14-year career with her childhood club.

"In Spain, football is the typical sport. When I was young, [it was] not for women, but fortunately, nowadays it is," said Putellas.

"I just had the ball at my feet and I was playing all the time - in the park, in the streets, sometimes at home.

"For me, it was normal because in my house Barca games were always on the TV. I started by watching games and then suddenly, I had the ball all day."

The 32-year-old went on to win 38 trophies with Barcelona, including 10 league titles and four European cups.

She was awarded back-to-back Ballon d'Or crowns in 2021 and 2022 and is favourite to win it again this year.

Internationally, she helped Spain win the 2023 World Cup and finish runners-up at Euro 2025.

But Putellas is not done. When asked if she can still get better, she laughed and said: "Yeah, of course. Always. Day after day, I want to learn things.

"That's the way I see this job. Just keep going, never stop and be as good as I can."

She described the journey she has embarked on at London City Lionesses as one that can help her "find where my limits are" as a footballer.

Putellas is enjoying pre-season but her focus never fully switches off.

"It's all about Manchester United," she says as she looks ahead to London City's season opener on 4 September (19:00 BST).

She has given up Champions League football to join London City, an independent women's-only club in its infancy. Will she need to adapt her mindset?

"Both can live together, my mentality and the moment of the project. I'm going to bring to the project whatever it needs from me," she added.

"I'm 100% committed. I'm hungry to win, I'm hungry to be better day after day and to fight with my team-mates for the victory."

Her competitiveness shines through in every conversation.

She is handed a present - a game based on the London underground - by BBC Sport.

"Oh yes, I will play with Freya Godfrey, then I can win. I will tell her that," she jokes.

That winning mentality has never changed - but she gained a new perspective when an anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury ruled her out of Euro 2022 on the eve of the tournament.

"Since the ACL injury, I enjoy everything. It's not enjoying just having fun, it's about learning something, and then I enjoy learning that thing," she added.

"I'm just a person who loves what she does. I love competition, I love football, I love training, I love to improve.

"I'm just always looking forward to better things and that's why I'm here too, because I always need to be moving as a person and a player."

Putellas is still learning the English language. She reminds journalists of that when she tries to breakdown the WSL's tactics.

"Sorry guys, I'm learning football language. This press conference maybe came early!" she jokes.

Her best friend and team mate Jana Fernandez will likely help her learn quickly, as well as several other Spaniards, including summer signing Mapi Leon from Barcelona.

But she has a better grasp of English than she realises and it is clear by the way she talks that her footballing brain is unique.

Her manager Eder Maestre says Putellas is like a secondary coach on the training pitch and has the ability to conduct the way the team plays.

"In my opinion, if I give you a pass without speaking, you have information. That's one thing I learned in Barcelona," she told the BBC.

"Maybe I am giving you that pass because I want them to receive a message like 'we go' or 'we stay.' If it's a stronger pass, it's for them to control or I want them to switch the game or whatever - it's just football language.

"Maybe I improved that in Barcelona because of the style of play. The best drills I ever trained in is about understanding what's happening in the game.

"If you understand what's happening in the game, you will get one step ahead of the opponents. When I'm training, I try to understand the way we want to play."

Putellas' fame is widespread and her grandeur was epitomised by her London City unveiling alongside billionaire owner Michele Kang in New York.

There was an emotional outpouring at her Barca departure on social media and she has 3.4m followers on Instagram.

A mural of Putellas dressed as a superhero was painted in her hometown and Nike gifted her a custom gold crown following her second Ballon d'Or victory.

"I try to not think about it, and just be like, I don't know if the word is normal, but just be me. For me, it's normal to be me," said Putellas.

She admitted walking into her first English press conference was "a little scary" and she does not generally enjoy being the centre of attention.

Her favourite part of the media day, she joked, was getting away from the cameras.

Even in the dressing room, where she is no doubt idolised by those around her, she says having former team-mates like Leon there "makes her feel more confident".

But despite the shyness, Putellas does not look out of place in the limelight. She has an obvious aura and instantly eases apprehension with humour.

In an exchange about her passing on her crown at Barcelona she quickly interjects: "No, I didn't have a crown! It's just media stuff!"

She adds: "I was just like another team-mate and so I feel like that, even if they call me 'La Reina.'

"I don't think anybody else needs to imagine 'I have a crown' and all of this because they are so good, they don't need anything from me.

"I just hope I left the team in a better position than when I started. That would make me feel so good and I enjoyed playing with them - I hope they enjoyed it as well."

Putellas' first few weeks at London City have been full of the challenges that most normal people experience - searching for a house, learning to drive in London, adapting to a new culture and developing her English.

"I have been looking for an apartment. [It's] not cheap. Well, in Barcelona, it's not cheap as well!" she said.

"Looking for where I have to go for shopping, just normal things that in Barcelona, of course, I knew. Now, here, everything is new. There's a lot of traffic here."

She has had family over to visit and has created a list of things to do in London with best friend and team-mate Fernandez.

Putellas was hoping to have dinner with England international and ex-Barcelona team-mate Keira Walsh last week but it had to be postponed.

Her friends in the WSL did give Putellas a warm welcome though...

"Well, some of them told me that it's a hard league and they're going to kick me! But no problem, I'm ready for that. No, I'm just joking...

"[They said] just enjoy the league because the games are crazy and even if you go to an away game, it's something different, something special."

Most of all, Putellas is learning to adapt to the English way of life.

She has tried a full English breakfast - but is not a fan of baked beans - and her TikTok algorithm is already throwing up typical conversational words like "innit".

"I tried an English breakfast. It's quite different from Spain. [I didn't like] the beans, but the sausages and eggs... It was fine," she joked.

"For Spanish people it's weird. Normally, we [have beans] with dinner or lunch, but not for breakfast. I don't know English culture yet!

"The weather is not bad now but I say that and people tell me, 'okay, wait for October and November.'"

But while Putellas is still adapting to life in England, it is clear she is ready to perform for London City Lionesses in September.

Her debut is likely to attract widespread attention and she hopes to embrace the occasion - after all, this is the challenge she craved.
